text:
I want to explore an AI tool that helps government agencies understand what needs to change when legislation, regulations or whole-of-government policies are updated. At the moment, staff often rely on emails, spreadsheets and individual knowledge to work out which internal policies, guidance, forms, systems and operational processes may be affected. This can take weeks and creates a risk that important dependencies are missed.

The tool would compare a new or amended requirement against an agency’s existing documents and produce a draft impact map. It would identify potentially affected obligations, documents, processes and business owners, explain why each item may be relevant and link its suggestions back to the source text. Policy, legal, compliance and operational staff could then review the map, reject false matches and assign confirmed actions.

It would use public legislation and policy material together with approved, unclassified internal documents. It would not provide authoritative legal advice, decide whether the agency is compliant or automatically change policies or systems. Human experts would remain responsible for interpreting requirements and approving any action. I imagine starting with one narrow policy area in a single agency to test whether the tool finds meaningful dependencies that staff would otherwise miss.

This sounds like a powerful way to reduce the 'institutional memory' bottleneck in policy implementation. I've drafted the core sections based on your description; to help us refine the scope, how do you envision the tool handling the 'versioning' of internal documents to ensure it's always comparing against the current state of the agency?

The tool should compare new requirements against a dated snapshot of the agency’s current, approved document set. Wherever possible, documents would come from an authoritative repository and retain metadata such as owner, approval status, version number, effective date and review date.

The AI should not silently decide which of several conflicting copies is current. If it finds duplicates, drafts or unclear version histories, it should flag them and ask an authorised user to confirm the version to include. Each impact map should record exactly which document versions were analysed so the result can be reproduced later.

When an internal document is updated, the tool would preserve the previous analysis and show what changed in the impact map rather than overwriting it. For an initial proof of concept, we could avoid live integration and use a manually curated, approved document set frozen at a nominated date.

That approach to versioning—treating the repository as a 'frozen' snapshot—is a smart way to manage risk and ensure auditability. Since we're prioritizing accuracy over live integration for the POC, how do you plan to handle the 'feedback loop' where the AI learns from the user's corrections to reduce false positives in future runs?
